analysis.one_liner: Requires debtors with income above set thresholds to repay creditors instead of wiping out debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one Democrat with no cosponsors, never left a House Judiciary subcommittee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a "means test" for personal bankruptcy. People whose income topped 75 percent of their state's median, and who could repay at least 20 percent of their unsecured debts over five years, would be barred from chapter 7 — the part of bankruptcy law that wipes out debts — and pushed into a five-year repayment plan instead. It also added new duties for bankruptcy trustees and gave debtors fee protection if a creditor wrongly tried to force them out of chapter 7.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers and other unsecured lenders, who would collect more from bankrupt households that the bill pushes into repayment plans instead of letting debts be discharged. Debtors who are wrongly accused of abusing chapter 7 would also gain a new rule making losing parties pay their legal fees.

how_it_helps.text: Bars individuals (or couples) whose combined monthly income exceeds 75 percent of their state's median family income, whose projected net income exceeds $50 a month, and who could repay 20 percent or more of their unsecured non-priority debts over five years from filing under chapter 7 liquidation [S2][S3].

Requires trustees to investigate and verify a debtor's reported monthly net income and to file reports with the court on whether the debtor qualifies for chapter 7, and whether plan payments should rise with income changes [S2][S3].
Gives debtors a shield: any party that moves to dismiss or convert a chapter 7 case as improper and loses must pay the debtor's reasonable attorney's fees and costs [S2][S3].
Allows debtors to claim extra expenses beyond the standard IRS allowance for 'extraordinary circumstances,' with detailed documentation and court review [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households above the income and repayment thresholds who would lose access to chapter 7's fresh start and instead pay into a five-year plan under IRS-standard expense budgets. All debtors would face added paperwork, investigation, and reporting costs, which typically raise the price of filing.

drawbacks.text: Debtors just above the thresholds would be locked into years of repayment calculated from IRS expense standards rather than their actual cost of living, unless they can document 'extraordinary circumstances' [S3].

The bill adds trustee investigations, sworn statements, itemized expense lists, and annual reporting, raising the cost and complexity of every bankruptcy case even for people who clearly qualify [S2][S3].
The bill's fee-shifting penalty on failed dismissal motions cuts the other way too: it could deter creditors from raising even legitimate eligibility challenges [S3].

A good-faith case for the bill: some filers with real ability to repay currently use chapter 7 to erase debts, and a means test could redirect that money to creditors and honest borrowers who pay their bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrower, more debtor-protective version of the means-test idea that creditors spent years promoting — it includes fee-shifting against abusive dismissal motions and an escape valve for unusual expenses. Still, its central effect is to take the bankruptcy fresh start away from households just above modest income and repayment thresholds, shifting money from struggling families to banks. The paperwork and investigation requirements would raise costs for everyone in the system. On balance, the burden falls on debtors and the benefit on lenders.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert E. Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the bill on January 19, 1999 [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On February 25, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where it stayed for the rest of the 106th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Struggling debtors who kept full access to chapter 7 debt relief, and no one else had to fight it — the bill simply never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alone on January 19, 1999; it never advanced past subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee and never held a markup or sent it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 25, 1999 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill would push above-median-income debtors from having their unsecured debts discharged into five-year repayment plans, moving money from bankrupt households to lenders. The lenders' gain is directly the debtor's loss.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy trustees and the bankruptcy court system
industries.note: Trustees would gain expanded duties — verifying debtor income, reporting to courts, monitoring income changes annually — funded within the existing system. Debtors and the courts would bear the added workload and cost of the new documentation requirements.
